transcript:
Header:
Date: 2028-06-15
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood), Jonah Reed (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Voss (Lattice SRE), Marcus Liu (Platform Eng), Priya Narang (Head of AI)
Recording note: automated transcription, medium quality, occasional mis-heard acronyms

Auto-summary (auto): Ephemeral KV backpressure from short-lived shards plus streaming fallthrough was identified as likely cause of p99 microbursts. Discussed mitigation: persistent shard warming, TTL-aware KV hotkey routing, bounded batching and streaming circuit-breaker, and reducing network hop count in VPC egress. Agreed to run controlled benchmark and share telemetry template and security docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: All right everybody thanks for joining, we're here to dig into the intermittent p99 spikes you saw last week. Jonah and I are from Redwood. Who wants to kick off with the symptom description?
[00:10] Dr. Elena Voss: Yeah thanks, so we've got this pattern where p50's nice, p95 is fine, but p99 this microburst every 15–20 minutes that lasts about 3 to 8 seconds. It coincides with a churn of short lived inference containers, and the KV cache seems to get hot then latency climbs.
[00:28] Marcus Liu: to add, we instrumented the prefix cache and saw TTL evictions and hotkey concentration from our batcher, not sure if it's a real hotkey or just ephemeral shard rebalancing when new pods register.
[00:40] Jonah Reed: Okay so the two immediate suspects: hotkey amplification on the KV shard, and network hop increases when a request falls through streaming to a non-streaming path. We often see streaming fallthrough add an extra hop to a fallback model or a compatibility endpoint.
[00:55] Priya Narang: Can you clarify streaming fallthrough? Is that when the streaming runtime can't match the model kv topology and reroutes?
[01:03] Jonah Reed: Yeah, roughly. In our runtime a streaming RPC tries to keep a lightweight path—KV local, pinned session—but if the session or shard isn't available we fall back to a non-streaming path that may rehydrate KV state and hit a different node, adding latency. That rehydration and kv fetch can blow out p99.
[01:22] Dr. Elena Voss: We also run VPC peering across regions for disaster recovery, could extra egress hops cause this?
[01:29] Maya Patel: Absolutely. Every additional network hop, NAT, or cross-zone hop increases jitter. We should look at the traceroutes during spike windows. Also check whether NAT timeouts are causing connection re-establishment.
[01:40] Speaker 1: (mumble) we had some nat gateway logs...
[01:45] Jonah Reed: So mitigation strategy—three levels: 1) Prevent spike formation at KV layer: persistent shard warmers, hotkey splitting or probabilistic jitter on caching TTLs; 2) Runtime routing: prefer colocated shard pinning and fast failover to warm replicas not to a cold rehydrate; 3) Circuit breakers on streaming: if streaming fallback rate exceeds X% we route to a dedicated non-streaming pool that is warmed.
[02:14] Marcus Liu: For hotkey splitting, do you mean consistent hashing changes, or application side sharding?
[02:19] Jonah Reed: We do consistent-hash aware sharding, but you can also do suffix hashing at app-layer like key_v2 = key || (hash(key) % N) to fragment heavy keys. Redwood recommends fragmenting only for the top 0.5% of keys.
[02:33] Dr. Elena Voss: There's also quantization: our ops team recently applied 4-bit quantization to one production model to shave cost. Could lower precision increase inference variance and maybe cause longer decode times that combine with KV rehydration to make tail events worse?
[02:46] Jonah Reed: Yes, quantization sometimes increases variability per-token for some models—especially those that rely on FP32 attention kernels. With int4, you can get increased decode variance and occasional fallback to FP16 kernels if numerical thresholds are hit, which means a slow path. That can exacerbate tail.
[03:05] Maya Patel: So the three-way interaction: quantization jitter + KV cold rehydrate + extra network hop = p99 spikes. We should instrument per-token kernel selection and mark those events in traces.
[03:15] Marcus Liu: How about batching windows? We currently use a 10ms microbatch and a 50ms macro-batch. Could changing those help?
[03:23] Jonah Reed: Yeah, batching affects latency vs throughput. For tail mitigation we recommend adaptive batching: shrink the batch window when queue depth is low, expand when high, and avoid head-of-line blocking by doing intra-batch pre-emption for streaming requests. In practice, moving microbatch to 5ms and enabling partial flushing on high-priority traffic lowered p99 in our tests.
[03:42] Priya Narang: Partial flushing—does that compromise throughput?
[03:44] Jonah Reed: Slightly, but you trade very small throughput for major p99 improvements. It's a controlled trade. Also enable prefix caching so repeated prefixes short-circuit generation.
[03:52] Dr. Elena Voss: Could you explain prefix caching vs KV cache? I think we use both terms loosely.
[03:57] Jonah Reed: Sure—prefix cache is application-level: if the start of a request matches a cached prefix we can skip a bunch of compute. KV cache is the model KV for KV-attention key-value cache across tokens for autoregressive models. Both help but operate at different layers.
[04:12] Maya Patel: Another operational mitigation is to reduce network hops: collocate KV shards with inference pods and ensure egress isn't traversing NAT gateways. For VPC setups, prefer ENIs and private link where possible.
[04:24] Marcus Liu: We're on a multi-tenant VPC with NAT gateways; moving to an ENI approach will need infra changes. Any best practices for gradual migration?
[04:31] Jonah Reed: Start by co-locating critical shards in the same AZ and test with canaries. You don't have to move everything at once. Also Redwood supports pinning for dedicated pools if you want guaranteed colocation.
[04:42] Speaker 2: (background) how about the autoscaler?
[04:44] Maya Patel: Good point—if autoscaling is too aggressive it causes churn. Use smoothing windows and prefer scale-up on CPU/throughput rather than pod count spikes, and add a cooldown to avoid oscillation.
[04:53] Dr. Elena Voss: We saw the autoscaler spin up 8 nodes in 30 seconds, that probably made things worse.
[04:57] Jonah Reed: Exactly—fast churn plus cold KV rehydrates = spike. OK let's talk metrics to collect. You should capture: per-shard hit rate, rehydrate latency, rehydrate byte counts, network hop counts, per-request path (streaming vs fallback), kernel selection events, quantization fallback counts, and batching window utilization. We'll provide a telemetry template.
[05:16] Marcus Liu: Can that be integrated into our datadog?
[05:18] Jonah Reed: Yes, the template is a set of traces and metrics you can push to Datadog; we'll also provide Grafana panels if you use Prometheus.
[05:24] Dr. Elena Voss: Any quick wins we can flip on today?
[05:27] Maya Patel: Short-term: 1) add a small jitter to TTL to avoid synchronized evictions, 2) reduce microbatch from 10ms to 5ms for streaming-heavy routes, 3) enable a warm replica routing policy for hot keys. Those are low risk.
[05:39] Priya Narang: Warm replica routing policy—what's the memory cost?
[05:42] Jonah Reed: Depends on model sizes and shard counts. Warm replicas keep KV warm so they hold larger memory footprints but you trade memory for tail stability. We can size it in the benchmark.
[05:51] Dr. Elena Voss: Let's talk benchmarks. We want a controlled run that reproduces p99. What inputs do you need?
[05:57] Jonah Reed: We'll need: representative request traces, traffic envelope (rps), routing config, quantization profile used, batch window settings, and a baseline where we disable streaming fallbacks so we can compare. We'll run the Redwood microbenchmark on your VPC or run a remote test against a dedicated pilot pool.
[06:14] Marcus Liu: We'd prefer to run inside our VPC on a canary subset.
[06:17] Maya Patel: Great. We'll provide an infra checklist and a benchmark spreadsheet. Link: https://redwood-internal.example/kv-benchmarks (note: placeholder link).
[06:26] Speaker 1: (laugh) that link might not open for you, it's internal sample.
[06:30] Jonah Reed: On security: you asked about KMS and SOC2. Redwood supports customer-managed KMS for private deployments and we provide SOC2 Type II artifacts. We'll attach those docs.
[06:40] Dr. Elena Voss: For on-prem/air-gapped: if we want a package what does that look like?
[06:45] Maya Patel: We have a private deployment bundle—control plane can be customer-managed; inference plane can be on-prem. It includes a hardened runtime, KMS connectors, and audit log shipping adapters. We'll send the private-deploy checklist.
[06:57] Priya Narang: Any gotchas for quantized models on on-prem hardware?
[07:01] Jonah Reed: On-prem GPUs vary. Some kernels for int4 quantization depend on vendor-specific CUDA/CUFFT optimizations. You should validate kernel availability on your hardware and we can provide a kernel matrix. Quantization may require specific driver versions.
[07:14] Marcus Liu: For the streaming circuit-breaker, do you have default thresholds?
[07:18] Jonah Reed: Default is failover at 3% fallback rate per minute or when average rehydrate latency exceeds 50ms. But tuning depends on SLOs.
[07:27] Dr. Elena Voss: Can we get recommendations aligned to our p99 target of 200ms?
[07:31] Jonah Reed: Yes—goal: keep combined rehydrate + network hop + kernel slow path < 80ms to leave buffer. So aim for rehydrate < 20–30ms and network hops < 1 extra hop ideally.
[07:45] Maya Patel: Recap of short term actions: Jonah will provide telemetry template and run a canary benchmark; Maya will send security + private deploy docs; Elena will gather traces and tcpdump for the next run.
[07:59] Dr. Elena Voss: We'll also try the microbatch change and TTL jitter in canary.
[08:04] Maya Patel: Great. Anything else?
[08:06] Priya Narang: One last thing—pricing for a warmed dedicated pool?
[08:09] Maya Patel: I'll put a sketch in email—ballpark for a small warmed pool for one AZ and N GPUs for pilot.
[08:17] Speaker 3: (background) thanks everyone
